headline: New England states join lawsuit over federal fuel-economy rule
dek: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont are among 26 states and local governments challenging NHTSA’s weaker mileage standards for new cars and light trucks.
body: Five New England states have joined a federal lawsuit challenging a new National Highway Traffic Safety Administration rule that lowers the fuel-economy requirements for new passenger cars and light trucks. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont are part of a coalition of 26 states, counties and cities that filed a petition for review Oct. 2 in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. The [Connecticut attorney general’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-challenges-trump-rollback-of-fuel-economy-standards) and [Vermont attorney general’s office](https://ago.vermont.gov/blog/2026/10/02/attorney-general-clark-joins-lawsuit-challenging-trump-administrations-rollback-fuel-economy) announced their states’ participation.

The case targets NHTSA’s final Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, rule. CAFE is a manufacturer-level program: automakers must meet an average fuel-economy requirement across the cars and light trucks they sell, rather than making every individual vehicle achieve one identical mileage figure. The agency’s [official program summary](https://www.nhtsa.gov/laws-regulations/corporate-average-fuel-economy) says the 2026 rule projects an industry fleetwide average requirement of about 34.9 miles per gallon in model year 2031. NHTSA also says it will end inter-manufacturer credit trading beginning in model year 2028 and revise fleet classifications beginning in 2030.

The states describe those changes as a weakening of long-standing requirements. In the petition, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell and the other parties argue that NHTSA failed to follow the Energy Policy and Conservation Act’s instruction to set standards at the “maximum feasible” level. They also allege that the agency’s analysis is arbitrary and capricious and violates the federal Administrative Procedure Act. Those are allegations in a pending case, not findings by the court.

The legal dispute turns partly on how the agency measured the existing vehicle fleet and the technology available to improve it. Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark’s office says the rule improperly requires NHTSA to ignore the presence of millions of electric vehicles when it evaluates what level of fuel economy is feasible. The [Massachusetts petition](https://www.mass.gov/doc/nhtsa-petition/download) says the coalition is challenging the rule’s treatment of fleet performance, fuel savings, vehicle affordability and related assumptions. NHTSA’s public summary presents the rule as an effort to bring the CAFE program into compliance with federal law.

The regional stakes are both practical and industrial. New England drivers would encounter the rule through the fuel efficiency of vehicles sold in coming model years, while manufacturers and dealerships would make product and compliance decisions under the revised standards. The states contend that weaker requirements can increase gasoline use and leave households more exposed to oil-price swings. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong’s office also points to the rule’s elimination of credit trading as a threat to electric-vehicle industries and other businesses that rely on a predictable national market. Those economic and consumer effects remain contested claims that the litigation will test.

The challenge arrives as the region is already pursuing its own transportation and climate policies. Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont have adopted or pursued vehicle-emissions rules that are more protective than federal baselines, while Connecticut and Maine are also participating in regional clean-transportation planning. A federal CAFE rule does not by itself cancel state air-pollution authorities, but it can change the nationwide floor for vehicle efficiency and complicate the market assumptions behind state programs. The lawsuit therefore reaches beyond a technical mileage formula into the states’ broader effort to reduce transportation emissions and fuel costs.

The coalition is led by California and includes attorneys general from states across the country, along with Chicago, Denver, New York City and the city and county of San Francisco. [California’s attorney general](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-bonta-files-lawsuit-challenging-trump-administration%E2%80%99s-rollback) listed the same 26-state-and-local-government coalition and said the petition was filed in the First Circuit. Independent coverage by [The Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/936f05f9284bf4ba49806b4a6070b8da) reported a separate lawsuit by environmental groups over the same federal rule, underscoring that the administration faces more than one legal challenge.

The new rule does not immediately change the mileage of cars already on New England roads, and the lawsuit does not by itself suspend the rule. The court could leave the standards in place while the case proceeds, or later order changes if the challengers prevail. The next important steps will be the federal government’s response and any request for a stay or other interim relief. Until the court acts, automakers, states and consumers will be watching how the revised standards are implemented and whether the First Circuit accepts the coalition’s argument that NHTSA set the bar below what federal law requires.
